talks.title: Diana Initiative 2025-Roxie Davis-Cyber Werewolves: Emulating the Enemy Before the Full Moon Rises
talks.teaser: Provides diana Initiative 2025-Roxie Davis-Cyber Werewolves: Emulating the Enemy Before the Full Moon Rises and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Roxie Davis presents at the Diana Initiative on "Cyber Werewolves," using the social deduction game metaphor to improve threat intelligence delivery to operational security teams.

Key Topics: 1987 werewolf/villager research on deception detection; mapping APT actors to werewolf roles; intelligence levels from strategic to tactical; and making intelligence actionable for SOC and IR teams.

Technical Details: Davis argues intelligence reports must be immediately actionable for operational teams rather than requiring analysts to extract relevant details. She compares ineffective intelligence to villagers ignoring werewolf warnings.

Takeaways: Threat intelligence fails when operational teams cannot immediately act on it. Intelligence producers should deliver tactical, ready-to-use findings rather than raw data requiring further analysis.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2025-HD Moore, Nicole Schwartz-Forging Strong Cyber Communities in Uncertain Times
talks.teaser: Demonstrates diana Initiative 2025-HD Moore, Nicole Schwartz-Forging Strong Cyber Communities in Uncertain Times and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Why communities exist

Nicole Schwartz opens by noting shared Defcon lunch experiences among underrepresented women in security, leading to groups where people with similar challenges support each other. HD Moore follows on building Metasploit amid early-2000s vendor retaliation and black-hat criticism.

How to start a community

Moore's playbook: register a name/domain, build something people want, then market relentlessly. Nicole adds polish matters—nonprofits can use Canva—and friction must stay low (e.g., pizza meetups where showing up is enough).

Rules, space, and growth

Borrow open-source codes of conduct, state expectations every meeting (no photos, no jerks), and provide Slack, Discord, or mailing lists with consistent communication. Surveys and positive messaging help underrepresented people see themselves in the mission; statistics support sponsorship.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2025-Aaron Stanely-Click Here Now: A Positive Way to Create Phishing Awareness
talks.teaser: Details diana Initiative 2025-Aaron Stanely-Click Here Now: A Positive Way to Create Phishing Awareness and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## The Problem with Shame

Aaron Stanley opens with a provocative claim: most phishing awareness programs fail because they punish users. Citing Brené Brown, he describes how shame convinces people they cannot change, undermining the security culture organizations claim they want.

## A Better Model

Stanley contrasts annual slide decks and gotcha simulations with positive, repeated practice—like California schools drilling earthquake response until behavior becomes instinct. Security training should build confidence and reflexes, not fear of HR consequences.

## Click Here Now

His team runs simulations that reward engagement and teach recognition without humiliation. The approach treats phishing defense as a skill developed over time, similar to emergency preparedness, rather than a compliance checkbox.

## Culture Over Blame

The talk urges security teams to stop treating users as the weakest link and start designing programs people actually want to participate in. Positive reinforcement, he argues, produces lasting behavior change that punitive campaigns never achieve.
